summary: MC-optimized hybrid structural speculative drafting with 5 strategies. v0.7.3 improvements: all-MC format detection (all 96 dev questions are MC), option sequence prediction (A→B→C→D at sentence boundaries, 65.9% acceptance), bigram fallback (29% acceptance, fills empty draft slots), smart period continuation (Option vs The based on context), enhanced MC templates (79 total), format-aware openings. Word-level simulation: 1.510x average speedup on MC responses (+24.7% over v0.6.0 baseline). All contract checks pass, deterministic, bounded O(1) cost per call.

strategies.name: prefix_grammar_templates
strategies.description: Matches end of decoded text against 79 MC-optimized templates. Highest-confidence structural triggers including answer-reveal, option analysis, reasoning transitions, and elimination patterns.
strategies.rationale: Visual reasoning models reliably produce structured answer-reveal phrases. These scaffolding tokens are highly predictable even when the specific answer content is not.
strategies.adaptation: Templates are adaptively re-ranked by observed acceptance rate. Best-performing triggers checked first. No hard suppression.
strategies.adaptation_note: Acceptance rate used in scoring; ranked_templates removed (dead code)

strategies.name: ngram_history_reuse
strategies.description: Searches backward through recent 150 words for repeated n-grams (n=2-3). Most effective on MC option enumeration patterns.
strategies.rationale: Multiple-choice reasoning enumerates options with parallel structure. N-gram reuse captures this without predefined templates. Less effective on free-form text.
strategies.adaptation: Per-strategy stats tracked. Strategy order can be adapted in future versions.

strategies.name: period_continuation_fallback
strategies.description: When decoded text ends with a sentence boundary (period), proposes 'The' as a high-frequency sentence starter. Cheap 1-token draft used only when higher-confidence strategies don't fire.
strategies.rationale: Better than zero draft when no stronger trigger matches. Minimal downside since it's only a single token.
strategies.adaptation: Per-strategy stats tracked. Acceptance rate informs ranking relative to other strategies.

strategies.name: opening_template
strategies.description: When decoded text is empty, proposes a domain-appropriate opening phrase. Uses MC-specific opening when multiple-choice options are detected in the question.
strategies.rationale: Visual reasoning models nearly always start with a framing sentence. The exact phrasing varies but the general form is predictable.

strategies.name: option_sequence_prediction
strategies.description: MC-specific: predicts next option letter (A→B→C→D) at sentence boundaries. Detects option pattern from last sentence (incorrect/correct/eliminated) and applies same pattern to next letter. Conservative: only fires at period boundaries with recent option mention.
strategies.simulated_acceptance_per_draft: 3.00 tokens (65.9% rate) — highest of any strategy
strategies.rationale: MC models enumerate options in order. After completing option analysis, the next sentence almost always starts with "Option [next letter]". Pattern matching captures the continuation verb (incorrect/correct/eliminated).
strategies.cpu_cost: ~20-40 µs (regex on last 60 words of text)
strategies.trigger_condition: sentence ends with period AND last sentence mentions an option AND not at option D

strategies.name: bigram_fallback
strategies.description: Last-resort 1-word continuation from static bigram table of MC visual reasoning common transitions. Never hurts since 0-accepted drafts are equivalent to empty proposals. Fills ~50 empty draft slots per response.
strategies.rationale: High-frequency function-word transitions are partially predictable. Even 30% acceptance on 1-word drafts adds meaningful speedup because there are many empty draft slots.

return_format: dict with 'text' field (trusted tokenizer encodes), or empty list for ordinary step

budget_handling.budget_application: draft_budget = min(remaining_tokens, maximum_draft_tokens, 32). Word-budget = max(1, draft_budget). Templates truncated to word_budget. Returns [] when budget <= 0.
budget_handling.note: Text-based proposals are not token-counted locally since the tokenizer is unknown. Uses word count as a conservative proxy (assumes ~1 token/word for common words). The trusted evaluator enforces the 32-token cap.

cpu_testbed_results.method: deterministic word-level simulation with 5 response formats, 20-30 seeds each

adaptive_history.note: adaptive didn't improve over static in single-sequence tests because templates are already well-chosen

testbed_hybrid.note: testbed hybrid underperforms on open-ended due to over-aggressive strategy disabling (important negative finding)

noise_robustness.description: Word-insertion noise simulates format deviation from expected structural patterns
noise_robustness.finding: All policies degrade gracefully. At 10% noise, ~70% of speedup remains. At 30% noise, ~20-30% remains. N-gram and grammar are similarly robust.

budget_sensitivity.finding: Most of the benefit comes from the first 4-8 draft tokens. Diminishing returns after 8 tokens.

cross_sequence_learning.finding: No measurable improvement when adaptive policy learns across 30 MC sequences. The template set is already near-optimal for this format.
cross_sequence_learning.implication: Adaptive learning is more valuable for variable-format workloads or when the template set is suboptimal.

what_cpu_simulation_predicts: Relative ordering of policy quality across formats with similar structure to real model outputs
That template-based structural drafting will provide measurable speedup on stereotyped reasoning text
That n-gram reuse will help most on highly repetitive formats (MC option enumeration)
That short draft lengths (4-8 tokens) capture most of the available structural benefit
That the policy will degrade gracefully as responses deviate from expected patterns
what_cpu_simulation_does_not_predict: Absolute real-world speedup numbers (no real tokenizer, no real model, word != token)
Acceptance rates on the long tail of unusual or creative model outputs
FP-numerical boundary effects between sequential and block target evaluation
Cache/compute overhead of the draft policy itself
Subword tokenization effects (our simulation uses whole-word tokens)
Exact acceptance rates — the simulation uses perfect format knowledge
Whether the real model uses the specific phrasing we've templated
assumptions: The target model produces English-language reasoning chains with stereotypical transition phrases.
The tokenizer is a standard subword tokenizer (BPE-like) where our short text templates encode to fewer than 32 tokens.
Multiple-choice questions follow standard A/B/C/D formatting patterns.
Acceptance of even 1-3 tokens per draft call provides meaningful latency reduction compared to always returning [].
The model uses temperature 0.6 sampling which produces reasonably deterministic structural transitions.
Word-level structural patterns in the simulation are qualitatively similar to token-level patterns in the real system.
generated_token_ids length accurately reflects decoding position (not including prompt tokens).
Draft state is evaluated by calling draft(state) sequentially as generation proceeds.

expected_failure_modes.description: Many templates propose only 1-4 tokens. If acceptance is low (<20%), draft verification overhead may outweigh savings.
expected_failure_modes.mitigation: Templates ordered by confidence; falls back to [] when no match rather than proposing low-confidence garbage.

expected_failure_modes.description: Text returned as {'text': ...} may tokenize to more tokens than expected, potentially exceeding the 32-token limit or producing suboptimal token boundaries.
expected_failure_modes.mitigation: All templates are short (<80 chars), well under any reasonable 32-token encoding. Word-budget truncation provides additional safety.

expected_failure_modes.description: Template matching uses lowercased text; case preservation of the continuation uses a heuristic based on trigger capitalization.
expected_failure_modes.mitigation: Case preservation checks the actual trigger word's capitalization in the original text. Most triggers are function words where case matters only at sentence boundaries.

expected_failure_modes.description: N-gram lookback may find coincidental matches that produce nonsensical continuations, especially with short n values.
expected_failure_modes.mitigation: Minimum n=2 (at least 2 word match). Only fires when higher-confidence grammar templates don't match. The target model verifies every token, so false drafts just cost one step.

expected_failure_modes.description: If the real model produces responses with very different phrasing than our templates assume, acceptance rates will be much lower than simulation predicts.
expected_failure_modes.mitigation: Templates are chosen for broad generality (common English reasoning phrases). Multiple strategies provide redundancy. Fallback to [] is always safe.

expected_failure_modes.description: Early in a session, with few observations, ranking may be based on noisy estimates and temporarily favor suboptimal templates.
expected_failure_modes.mitigation: Conservative 5-draft minimum before using acceptance stats. All templates remain eligible as fallback.

next_discriminating_gpu_experiment.name: paired_seed_acceptance_with_adaptation
next_discriminating_gpu_experiment.description: Run the policy on paired seeds (17, 29, 43, 71, 101) and measure per-draft acceptance count, number of draft calls, and end-to-end latency. Compare against baseline (empty draft).
next_discriminating_gpu_experiment.why_discriminating: This is the single most informative experiment: it measures actual acceptance rate on the real model, which directly determines whether structural drafting provides any benefit. A low acceptance rate (<0.3 tokens/draft) would indicate our template assumptions are wrong and we need to pivot strategies.
key_metrics: average accepted tokens per draft call
output agreement check (must match baseline exactly)
next_discriminating_gpu_experiment.expected_outcome_if_hypothesis_correct: 1.05-1.2x speedup, 0.5-1.5 average accepted tokens per draft call, 100% output agreement
next_discriminating_gpu_experiment.what_would_surprise_us: Acceptance rate <0.2 tokens/draft (templates don't match real output), or output disagreement (FP numerical issues in block evaluation)
next_discriminating_gpu_experiment.adaptation_questions: Does online adaptation improve acceptance rate on the real model? How quickly does trigger ranking converge? Does cross-question transfer work across real questions?

online_adaptation.description: Infers how many draft tokens were accepted by computing len(generated_token_ids) delta between consecutive draft() calls, minus 1 (the ordinary fallback token from the target model). No access to target logits or private state needed — uses only the public draft(state) interface.
adaptation_actions: Reorder templates by observed acceptance rate (proven good → unknown → proven poor)
Select among matching templates by expected value (acceptance_rate * continuation_length)
Conservative: only rank after 5+ observations per trigger
what_is_NOT_adapted: No hard suppression of low-performing triggers (all remain eligible)
No global draft length factor (found to be harmful in testing)
No strategy disabling (found to hurt more than help)

complexity.state_memory: ~600 bytes (bounded by fixed template set size)
complexity.per_call_ops: O(n_templates) for ranking, O(1) for observation

state_leakage_risks.description: Per-trigger stats persist across questions. Could bias early drafts of a new question toward the previous question's format.
state_leakage_risks.mitigation: Conservative ranking (5+ observations before trusting stats). Recent window resets per question. Bias is toward better-performing templates which should generalize.

state_leakage_risks.description: If generated_token_ids includes prompt tokens or special tokens, acceptance inference will be wrong.
state_leakage_risks.mitigation: Sanity checks: accepted >= 0, accepted <= proposed. Conservative ranking thresholds tolerate some noise. Wrong inference just means slower adaptation, not incorrect behavior.

state_leakage_risks.description: Might incorrectly reset per-question state. Just loses history — safe.
state_leakage_risks.mitigation: Multiple redundant reset signals. False positive is safer than false negative.

state_leakage_risks.risk: Tokenizer mismatch in proposed token estimate
state_leakage_risks.description: We estimate proposed tokens as word count, but real tokenizer uses subwords.
state_leakage_risks.mitigation: Only used for sanity cap (accepted <= proposed). Word count <= token count is conservative. Position delta itself uses real token IDs and is accurate.

cache_rollback_verification.summary: Independent KV-cache + speculative verification simulator with 10 invariants, 1000 randomized differential tests, 5000-token stress test. All invariants hold.
verified_invariants: cache_prefix_matches_oracle (cache content always matches oracle prefix
bonus_implies_full_accept (bonus token only added when all draft tokens accepted)

holds_for: full acceptance with bonus (delta = accepted + 1 bonus)

edge_case_eos_in_draft.behavior: When EOS is accepted within the draft (not as bonus), delta = accepted exactly (no extra token). Formula undercounts by 1.
edge_case_eos_in_draft.frequency: Once per question, on the final step only
edge_case_eos_in_draft.impact_on_adaptation: negligible — one data point per question, conservative undercount is safe
edge_case_eos_in_draft.mitigation: max(0, accepted) clamping already handles it; result is conservative

edge_case_bonus_overshoot.behavior: Bonus token can push output past max_tokens by 1. If evaluator clips strictly, delta = accepted on final full-accept step.
edge_case_bonus_overshoot.frequency: Depends on draft alignment with max_tokens boundary
edge_case_bonus_overshoot.impact_on_adaptation: negligible — at most one step per question

randomized_testing.stress_test: 5000-token sequence, 3239 steps, 2959 rollbacks — all invariants hold

key_findings: CPU policy overhead is 0.001-0.02x of GPU step cost — negligible
All strategies are worth keeping; each needs only ~0.003 extra tokens/draft to justify cost
n-gram max_n=3 is as good as n=5 or n=7 across all 5 test formats
150-word n-gram window captures 100% of matches up to 800-word histories
ranked_templates was dead code — reordering has no effect when all are scored
Break-even acceptance varies 0.4-0.8 depending on GPU batch efficiency profile
Optimal draft length: N=1 at p<0.3, N=3-7 at p=0.5-0.7, N=14-26 at p=0.9
Adaptive block control (slow window) gains ~2-3% over best static on heterogeneous content
simplifications_v050: n-gram window: 150 words (bounded cost, no quality loss at <128 tokens)
Removed ranked_templates call (dead work, 1.37x faster matching)

fp_numerical_sensitivity.key_correction_from_v1: Initial audit used 3e-5 relative as 'BF16 scale' — this is ~150x too small. True BF16 ULP is ~0.5-0.8% relative (7 mantissa bits).
fp_numerical_sensitivity.flip_rate_scaling: Roughly linear with ULP count: ~1% per ULP for medium distribution

our_policy_risk_assessment.verdict: SAFE — FP noise is negligible compared to normal acceptance variance
why_safe: Template tokens have large decision margins (median 4+ log/temp units)
Draft lengths are short (2-4 tokens for templates)
FP flips cause at most 1 extra rejection step per draft
Rejection overhead is small relative to potential speedup

safeguard_analysis.logit_gap_filtering_effectiveness: low — Gumbel noise dominates decision margin; deterministic logit gap is a weak predictor of flip probability
safeguard_analysis.position_0_reuse: minor benefit (~6% reduction in any-flip for N=8), cheap to implement
safeguard_analysis.fp32_sampling: potentially effective if sampling step is FP source, but most error likely in logit computation
safeguard_analysis.shorter_drafts: linear reduction in flip rate, linear cost in speedup
recommended_safeguards_for_production: Position-0 logit reuse from autoregressive cache (free, minor benefit)
Keep draft lengths moderate (<=8 for high-confidence, <=4 for medium)

replay_dynamics.verdict: Negligible — FP does not cause problematic replay loops

what_cpu_simulation_cannot_prove: Whether error grows with position index
Correlation structure of errors across positions
Whether causal mask is correct in block attention
Exact template acceptance rates on real model

uncertainties: Real template acceptance rates on actual model outputs (word-level sim is approximate)
Format detection from decoded text catches MC early enough (first 1-2 options)?
Adaptive truncation thresholds: current values are reasonable defaults, not GPU-optimized
N-gram effectiveness on real model outputs (depends on actual structural repetition)
FP noise impact on real GPU: block-vs-sequential logit diff magnitude unknown
Opening template acceptance rate: does "Looking at the image" always start the response?
Token vs word budget mismatch: real tokenizer may split differently
Adaptation convergence speed across diverse question types

format_aware_ordering.description: Detects MC reasoning from question text AND decoded text (last 1200 chars). Uses n-gram-first strategy for MC (better on repetitive structure), template-first for open-ended (better on transition phrases).
format_aware_ordering.expected_improvement: 5-15% relative on MC, neutral on open-ended

adaptive_draft_length.description: Truncates draft continuation based on trigger confidence. Known high acceptance (>=50%): full length. Medium (>=30%): up to 4w. Low (>=15%): up to 2w. Unknown: up to 5w cap.
adaptive_draft_length.mechanism: _adaptive_truncate() called after template match and case preservation
adaptive_draft_length.rationale: Maximizes expected accepted tokens per verification step. Shorter drafts have higher acceptance; match ambition to confidence.

types_added: option X is → incorrect because (4 variants: A,B,C,D)
option X is incorrect because → the (4 variants)
option X is correct because → the (4 variants)

all_mc_discovery.description: All 96 dev questions are multiple-choice across 6 categories. Confirmed via samples.json analysis.
formats: short_mc (71 questions, Options: A: B: C: D:)

option_sequence_prediction.description: New strategy: predicts next option letter at sentence boundaries with same analysis pattern. Conservative trigger: only at periods with recent option mention.
option_sequence_prediction.result: 65.9% acceptance rate, 3.00 accepted tokens/draft — highest of any strategy

bigram_fallback.description: 1-word static bigram table as last-resort filler. 25 common MC transitions.
bigram_fallback.result: 29.2% acceptance, fills ~48 empty slots/response. Pure upside (0-accepted = same as empty).

smart_period_continuation.description: Period continuation predicts "Option" when in MC analysis mode (2+ recent option mentions), "The" otherwise.

enhanced_templates.description: Extended from 48 to 79 templates with more MC-specific patterns: answer reveals, elimination patterns, reasoning transitions.

tested_and_rejected: Trigram+bigram combined: slightly worse than bigram-only (1.506x vs 1.510x) — hand-curated trigram table not accurate enough
Dynamic bigram from history: worse than static (25.2% vs 30.7%) — not enough history in short responses
Generic "option" template: wrong more often than right (fires before option letter), but 0-accepted so no harm
n-gram max_words tuning: no difference — proposals already short
